title: The Hard Word
full_review:
Three recently paroled brothers find it difficult to shake their criminal ways in the Aussie crime drama, "The Hard Word" (Lions Gate).

While first-time director Scott Robert's hard-boiled yarn boasts a gritty noir look and interesting characters, the movie is ultimately undermined by the filmmaker's morally bankrupt suggestion that crime does pay.

The story revolves around a trio of ex-con siblings, the Twentyman brothers, who have just finished serving time in an Australian prison for armed robbery. Dale (Guy Pearce), the eldest, is the brains and lead dog of the operation. Cheery middle brother Mal (Damien Richardson) is a sensitive bloke whose culinary skills had made him popular among his fellow inmates. The youngest, Shane (Joel Edgerton), is a muscular time bomb prone to unpredictable fits of rage.
As soon as they hit the streets of Sydney, the Twentyman boys are back doing what they do best: holding-up armored cars. Divvying up the loot, they discuss their plans for the future. Dale wants to retire to a life of leisurely reading in the countryside with his wife Carol (Rachel Griffiths), a femme fatale with bleached-blond hair and a black-widow smile. Mal dreams of opening up a butcher shop. Shane dreams of working on his pecs.

The mates soon find themselves back in the slammer. Dale harbors suspicions that their crooked attorney, Frank Malone (Robert Taylor), is to blame. Dale also suspects that Carol is making as many conjugal visits to the unctuous lawyer's office as she is to the prison.

Malone cautions patience, assuring the troika that he has the contacts to get them out, but there's a hitch. They must pull off one last job before bowing out of the business -- a job that will guarantee them retirement security. The jackpot involves fleecing high rollers at the ultra-posh Melbourne Cup, a horserace with a multimillion-dollar purse. Due to the ambitious scope of the operation, Malone insists the brothers take two hired guns on board -- one of them a trigger-happy psycho named Tarzan (Dorian Nikono). Dale realizes they are being set-up so that Malone can make off with both the money and Carol.

The narrative quickly unravels into a game of follow the bag of money, as the brothers, Malone and Carol all become entangled in a web of double-crossings and deceit, capped off by a darkly humorous "Sweeney Todd"-type finale that would make Hannibal Lecter drool with envy.

On one level "The Hard Word," with its well-choreographed heist and frenetic getaway sequence, differs little from countless other caper flicks, yet this movie is much more about the characters and their relationship to each other.

Shoot-'em-up sequences are relegated to the peripheral of the narrative and seem almost out of place when they come to the fore.

While many of the supporting players are rather two-dimensional, the synergy between the Twentyman kin affords them a depth of character atypical to the genre. The fact that they are crooks is almost irrelevant, since the subtext they share as brothers is much more engaging than their surface criminality.

What is troublesome about this film is not that the "heroes" live by a criminal code -- such anti-heroes are a staple of the pulp crime lexicon -- but rather the problematic bone which the movie leaves viewers gnawing on. As the curtain drops on the final slow-motion image of the brothers' smug swagger, it seems that the intended message is that not only can you get away with murder, but that it can be quite lucrative.

Due to recurring graphic violence, much rough language and profanities, instances of fleeting nudity, as well as an implied sexual encounter, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
